facts.t: The Unitarian Church at the top of Church Street has stood since 1816 — its organ arrived from Boston by sleigh
Burlington was chartered on June 7, 1763 — a full century before it incorporated as a city in 1865
Ethan Allen and the Green Mountain Boys took Fort Ticonderoga without a battle on May 10, 1775
Church Street closed to cars in 1980 after a one-day 1971 street fair drew 15,000 people
The world's second commercial steamboat, the Vermont, was built on Burlington's waterfront and launched in 1809
With about 44,700 people, Burlington is the smallest U.S. city that is its state's largest
P.T. Barnum offered $50,000 in 1873 for the hide of Champ, Lake Champlain's fabled monster
A day and a half in Copenhagen in 1962 gave architect Bill Truex the idea for the Church Street Marketplace
Ira Allen donated 50 acres to found the University of Vermont in 1791 — the same year Vermont became a state
During the War of 1812, Burlington's military camp held up to 5,000 troops — more than the town's own population
Ben & Jerry's scooped its first cone in 1978 from a renovated gas station in downtown Burlington
City Hall's 1928 building came from McKim, Mead & White — the firm behind Manhattan's original Penn Station
Smugglers aboard the Black Snake killed three revenue men on the Winooski River in 1808 — 10,000 watched the hanging that followed
Bernie Sanders won Burlington's 1981 mayoral race by ten votes, a margin that survived a recount
Andrew Carnegie paid $50,000 to build the Fletcher Free Library, the first of Vermont's four Carnegie libraries
For 18 days in March 1998, Lake Champlain was legally one of America's Great Lakes
Phish formed at UVM in 1983 and played their first gig in a campus dining hall that December
Gunners at Battery Park helped drive off a British squadron on Lake Champlain in August 1813
Philosopher John Dewey was born in Burlington in 1859 and graduated Phi Beta Kappa from UVM in 1879
In 1979 Winooski seriously studied covering the entire city with a dome to cut heating bills
By the 1870s Burlington's waterfront ranked as the third-largest lumber market in the world
The Marquis de Lafayette himself laid the cornerstone of UVM's Old Mill on June 29, 1825
Urban renewal erased Burlington's Little Italy in the 1960s, displacing 167 families; a marker finally went up in 2011
Ethan Allen spent his final years farming along the Winooski River and is buried in Burlington's Green Mount Cemetery
The Fletcher Free Library was built over a filled-in ravine — by 1973 it was sinking and nearly demolished
Burlington became the first U.S. city to run on 100 percent renewable electricity after buying a Winooski River dam in 2014
The Moran Plant burned coal from 1954 to 1986, then reopened in 2022 as the FRAME, a stripped-to-steel public pavilion
American and British fleets clashed at Valcour Island on Lake Champlain in October 1776
Buildings along Battery Street date to the 1790s, when the neighborhood grew up around Burlington's first wharves
Founded in 1791, UVM is the fifth-oldest university in New England
Union Station opened in 1916, shared by two railroads — its 1867 predecessor was demolished the next year
Ben & Jerry's began with a $12,000 investment and a Penn State correspondence course in ice cream making
A 1989 Vermont Supreme Court ruling under the public trust doctrine helped Burlington reclaim its waterfront for the public
The Allen brothers' Onion River Company bought up the land that became Burlington in the 1770s
The Burlington Breakwater, begun in 1836, is a rare surviving 19th-century timber-crib breakwater on the National Register
Free Cone Day started in 1979 as Ben & Jerry's first-anniversary thank-you to Burlington
Amelia Earhart met 4,000 schoolchildren at Memorial Auditorium; Duke Ellington and Nina Simone played there in the '60s
From the 1880s to World War II, Burlington's Old North End was 'Little Jerusalem,' a Yiddish-speaking quarter with three synagogues
Phish played their first Nectar's shows in late 1984 — the club that launched them closed in 2025 after 50 years
Lake Champlain stretches 107 miles and plunges 400 feet at its deepest point
Nearly every finish on the 1928 City Hall — brick, marble, slate, granite — was produced in Vermont
UVM's Phi Beta Kappa chapter was the first in America to admit women, in 1875, and African Americans, in 1877
Burlington's 300-bed military hospital was the largest in the Champlain Valley during the War of 1812
Buckminster Fuller flew in for Winooski's 1980 dome symposium before Washington pulled the plug
The wreck of the 1876 canal schooner General Butler lies near the breakwater — now a favorite dive site
Burlington swapped coal for wood: the McNeil wood-chip power plant replaced the aging Moran Plant in 1984
